__data__.text:
Sumati, the ruler of Visala, warmly welcomes Sage Viswamitra and respectfully inquires about Sri Rama and Lakshmana.
He praises their noble appearance, likening their strength and grace to that of gods, and admires their youth, valor, and striking presence.
Sumati expresses curiosity about their purpose, eager to understand why these extraordinary youths, carrying powerful weapons, have come to his land.
In response, Viswamitra recounts the recent events, explaining their journey, the challenges faced,
and the defeat of an ogress at Siddhasrama. Sumati, amazed, honors Sri Rama and Lakshmana with
great respect as guests of high distinction. After a restful night in Visala, they depart for Mithila the following day.
On the way, Sri Rama notices an abandoned but beautiful hermitage and asks Viswamitra about its history.
Viswamitra, in response, begins to share the tale of the hermitage’s former resident, the revered sage Gautama,
who once lived there with his wife, Ahalya, before the site was cursed.

__data__.text:
In response to Sri Rama’s inquiry, Sage Viswamitra narrates the story of the hermitage,
once belonging to the revered sage Gautama. Known for his spiritual strength, Gautama lived here with his wife, Ahalya,
dedicating himself to long years of austerity. During one of Gautama’s absences, Indra, disguised as the sage, approached Ahalya,
who, although recognizing Indra, was misled and allowed herself to be deceived.
When Gautama returned and found Indra, he was deeply angered. Gautama cursed Indra, causing him to lose his power,
and also pronounced a curse on Ahalya, sentencing her to live unseen by others, surviving on air alone, and lying in ashes,
repenting for many years. However, Gautama foretold that she would be freed from this curse upon being visited by Sri Rama,
after which she would regain her true form and return to him. Having spoken, Gautama departed to the Himalayas to continue his penance,
leaving the hermitage abandoned.

__data__.text:
Upon being deprived of his virility due to Sage Gautama’s curse, Indra, feeling remorseful, approaches the gods,
including Agni and celestial beings, seeking restoration of his manhood. The gods, understanding Indra's predicament,
appeal to the celestial manes, offering a ram as a replacement for Indra's lost virility. The manes agree and transfer the ram’s attributes
to Indra, granting him renewed wholeness.
At Sage Viswamitra’s request, Sri Rama, along with Lakshmana, enters Gautama’s hermitage. There, they encounter Ahalya,
whose celestial form shines with the radiance of her penance. Once hidden from the view of all beings due to the curse,
Ahalya is finally visible, marking the end of her long period of penance. The sight of Sri Rama brings her release from the curse,
and her presence becomes perceptible to the world again, restored by the virtues of the great sage’s blessings and Rama’s arrival.

__data__.text:
Sri Rama, led by Sage Viswamitra and accompanied by Lakshmana, enters Sage Gautama’s hermitage and sees Ahalya.
She appears radiant, her form enhanced by her penances, yet previously hidden from sight due to Gautama’s curse.
Now, with Sri Rama’s arrival, her form becomes visible again, marking the end of the curse.
As Sri Rama and Lakshmana greet her, Ahalya welcomes them, recalling Sage Gautama’s prophecy about her liberation.
She offers them water and honors them in accordance with traditional rites, which Sri Rama accepts graciously. A shower of flowers from
the heavens follows, accompanied by celestial drums, as gods, Gandharvas, and nymphs celebrate Ahalya's liberation.
The gods commend her for her pure state, achieved through her penance, and her renewed alignment with Gautama.
Sage Gautama, now reunited with Ahalya, is also content and resumes his ascetic practices. Sri Rama, having received Gautama’s blessings,
continues his journey to Mithila, honored by all at the hermitage.

__data__.text:
Sri Rama and Lakshmana, led by Sage Viswamitra, journey north-east from the hermitage and reach the sacrificial site of King Janaka of Mithila.
Rama marvels at the impressive preparations for the sacrifice, observing the presence of countless learned Brahmins and enclosures for sages,
filled with the necessities for their sacred rituals. Rama asks Viswamitra to find a suitable place for their stay,
to which Viswamitra selects a serene spot with water, where they settle.
Upon hearing of Viswamitra’s arrival, King Janaka, accompanied by his family priest Satananda and other esteemed priests,
hurriedly arrives to greet the sage. Janaka, with deep respect, performs the traditional rites and offers Viswamitra hospitality,
which the sage graciously accepts. Viswamitra inquires about Janaka’s well-being and the progress of the sacrifice,
and he warmly greets the other sages and priests present. With humility, Janaka offers Viswamitra a seat, along with his fellow sages,
and everyone, including the king and his ministers, take their places around him.
King Janaka then speaks to Viswamitra, expressing gratitude for the sage’s presence, considering it a blessing and a fulfillment
of his sacrificial efforts. Janaka feels deeply honored by Viswamitra’s arrival and notes that his sacrificial vow will continue for
twelve more days, during which time, he believes, the gods will appear for their share of offerings. Janaka then turns to Viswamitra and,
with great curiosity, asks about the identity of the two noble youths, Sri Rama and Lakshmana, noting their divine-like valor and youthful elegance.

__data__.text:
After Sage Viswamitra took his seat, King Janaka, along with his family priest Satananda and other dignitaries,
gathered around him. Addressing Viswamitra, Janaka expressed his gratitude for the sage’s presence,
viewing it as a divine fulfillment of his sacrificial preparations. The king felt that the mere sight of Viswamitra and the accompanying sages
had blessed the sacrificial grounds. With humility, Janaka mentioned that the sacrificial vow would continue for twelve more days,
after which he hoped the gods would appear to claim their offerings.
Janaka then looked upon the young princes, Rama and Lakshmana, with admiration. He remarked on their godlike valor,
their noble bearing, and their resemblance to divine beings who seemed to have descended from the heavens. Observing their lotus-like eyes,
strong posture, and youthful grace, Janaka wondered who these two radiant warriors were, whose demeanor and appearance were strikingly alike,
as if they were mirror images of one another. Eager to know more, Janaka asked Viswamitra about their lineage and the purpose of their visit.
Responding to Janaka's questions, Viswamitra revealed that Rama and Lakshmana were sons of King Dasaratha of Ayodhya.
He recounted the princes’ courageous journey, their victory over demons at Siddhasrama, their visit to the city of Visala,
their respectful meeting with Sage Gautama, and their arrival in Mithila. He explained that their journey also aimed to witness and,
perhaps, test the divine bow possessed by Janaka—a test offered to those desiring his daughter’s hand in marriage.
Having shared this background, Viswamitra paused, allowing the assembled listeners to absorb the remarkable journey
and deeds of the two young princes.

__data__.text:
Upon hearing Viswamitra’s account, Satananda, the son of Sage Gautama and an ascetic of great brilliance,
felt profound astonishment and joy at the sight of Sri Rama. Observing the two princes, Rama and Lakshmana, seated comfortably,
Satananda addressed Viswamitra, asking if his mother, Ahalya, had indeed received Rama’s grace and if she had honored him with
hospitality during his visit. He inquired if Viswamitra had shared Ahalya’s story with Rama,
and if her reunion with Gautama was truly due to Rama’s presence. Satananda expressed hope that both his
mother and father had honored Rama, appreciating his noble presence with tranquility and respect.
In response, Viswamitra assured Satananda that he had fulfilled his responsibilities, revealing that Ahalya and Gautama
had been joyfully reunited, similar to how Renuka, the mother of Parasurama, had reconciled with her husband Jamadagni.
Satisfied with this answer, Satananda turned to Rama, warmly welcoming him to Mithila. He recognized Rama’s arrival as a blessing,
especially as he had come under the guidance of Viswamitra, a sage of unconquerable spirit and unmatched ascetic power.
Satananda spoke of Viswamitra’s remarkable journey, his unparalleled achievements in austerities,
and his transformation into a Brahmarshi—a status attained through dedication and spiritual depth. In his admiration,
he remarked that no one was as fortunate as Rama, for Viswamitra himself had become his guide.
He then began to recount the life and power of Viswamitra, offering to reveal all that was remarkable about this great sage and his path.

__data__.text:
Hearing Viswamitra’s response, the radiant Satananda began to speak to Rama, warmly welcoming him to Mithila and
acknowledging the great fortune of having Viswamitra, an undefeated sage of immense power, accompany him.
Satananda expressed awe for Viswamitra's accomplishments, his ascetic strength, and his attainment of the revered Brahmarshi status.
He praised Rama as the most blessed of all, having Viswamitra, the son of Kusika, as his guardian.
Satananda then began recounting Viswamitra's illustrious ancestry and accomplishments. He explained that Viswamitra,
born into the lineage of Kusa, son of Brahma, was a king who ruled for thousands of years before his transformation into a sage.
He described how Viswamitra, accompanied by a grand army, traveled across cities, rivers, mountains, and hermitages
until reaching the sacred site of Sage Vasistha’s ashram. This hermitage was a haven filled with various flowers, trees, peaceful animals,
and divine beings like Gandharvas and Kinnaras. It was frequented by celestial beings and sages, creating an atmosphere
that resembled Brahmaloka.
The hermitage was populated by holy sages, some of whom sustained themselves on air, water, leaves, or simple forest foods.
These sages were deeply devoted, practicing intense austerities and mastering both their physical and mental faculties.
This gathering of great souls and ascetics, devoted to sacred rituals, further elevated the place's sacredness.
As Satananda recounted, Viswamitra gazed upon this sacred haven, taking in its profound spiritual beauty.

__data__.text:
Delighted to see Sage Vasistha, the revered Viśvāmitra approached him with respect, bowing in humility.
Vasistha welcomed Viśvāmitra warmly and offered him a seat, presenting fruits and roots in line with customary hospitality.
Gratefully accepting this, Viśvāmitra inquired about the welfare of Vasistha’s disciples, his worship rituals,
and the flourishing of plants in the hermitage. In response, Vasistha assured him that all was well.
As they conversed, Vasistha kindly asked Viśvāmitra about his own kingdom, whether he ruled with righteousness
and ensured the well-being of his people, family, allies, and treasury. Viśvāmitra, with deep respect,
affirmed that everything was in harmony in his realm. Their shared conversations, filled with wisdom and respect,
brought both sages immense joy.
At the end of their discussions, Vasistha offered to host Viśvāmitra and his entire army with a hospitality worthy of his status,
earnestly requesting him to accept this gesture. Viśvāmitra, though deeply touched, humbly declined, acknowledging the honor
he already received from Vasistha’s words, hospitality, and the sacred environment of the hermitage.
He expressed his gratitude and prepared to depart with a respectful farewell, hoping that Vasistha would always regard him with kindness.

__data__.text:
After an extended conversation that filled them both with joy, Sage Vasistha and King Viśvāmitra felt mutual contentment and respect.
At the close of this exchange, Vasistha, expressing warmth and hospitality, invited Viśvāmitra to accept a more elaborate
welcome along with his entire retinue. He emphasized the honor he felt in hosting such a distinguished guest.
Although initially humble in his response, Viśvāmitra graciously accepted this offer out of respect for Vasistha’s generous spirit.
Vasistha, overjoyed, called upon his miraculous cow, Sabala, who possessed the ability to fulfill any wish,
to prepare a lavish meal to honor Viśvāmitra and his troops. He requested Sabala to conjure all types of food and drink
to satisfy every preference, providing a complete feast to reflect the honor and respect he wished to convey to his esteemed guest.

__data__.text:
In response to Vasistha’s command, the cow Sabala, renowned for her magical abundance,
miraculously produced every delicacy desired by each member of Viswamitra’s camp. She provided sugarcane, honey, fried grains, exotic wines,
and various fine beverages and foods, leaving everyone completely satisfied. Vast heaps of steaming rice, fragrant rice cooked in milk,
flavorful pulses, curds, ghee, and plates of sweets and fruit juices appeared in abundance.
Viswamitra and his entire army, along with his ministers, advisors, and priests, were honored and gratified by the lavish hospitality.
In a joyful state, Viswamitra expressed his gratitude to Vasistha and, as a gesture of appreciation, requested Sabala,
offering a hundred thousand cows in exchange. He reasoned that such a valuable creature rightly belonged with a king.
However, Vasistha politely declined, explaining that no amount of wealth could compensate for Sabala’s worth.
She was central to his life, supporting his rituals, spiritual practices, and daily sustenance. Sabala was indispensable to him,
not merely as a provider but as a symbol of his spiritual commitment and personal fulfillment.

__data__.text:
Viswamitra, enchanted by Sabala’s powers, pressed Vasistha once more to give her to him, claiming that as a king,
he was the rightful recipient of such a valuable being. Vasistha, however, maintained his stance firmly,
declaring that he would not relinquish Sabala, no matter the offer. Sabala was indispensable to him—not just as
a source of sustenance but also as the spiritual and ritual cornerstone of his life.
Despite Viswamitra’s persistence, Vasistha was unyielding, explaining that Sabala’s presence enabled his sacrifices and daily rites,
sustaining his spiritual practices. The cow represented not only his material wealth but also his life force, integral to his existence
and religious devotion. Viswamitra then increased his offer, promising elephants adorned in gold, chariots, horses of fine lineage,
and a crore of cows, yet Vasistha remained resolute. He declared that Sabala was his only treasure, his true wealth,
and he would never part with her, as she was the foundation of his religious duties and his very life.

__data__.text:
When Sage Vasistha refused to give up his cow, Sabala, Viswamitra decided to seize her by force and take her to his capital.
As Sabala was being dragged away, she grew distressed and sorrowful, wondering if she had been abandoned by her master, Vasistha.
Deeply hurt and crying, she freed herself from Viswamitra’s retainers and hurried back to Vasistha.
Once before him, Sabala, with a voice heavy with sorrow, questioned if she had been forsaken, given that the king’s soldiers
were taking her away from his presence. Vasistha, seeing her in such despair, reassured Sabala, explaining that he had not abandoned her
and that she had done no wrong. Rather, Viswamitra, driven by his power as a mighty Kshatriya king, was using force to take her away.
With his formidable army of chariots, elephants, and horses, Viswamitra’s power was indeed strong.
However, Sabala reminded Vasistha that the spiritual strength of a Brahmana was greater than the physical might of a Kshatriya.
She affirmed his unmatchable strength and urged him to command her to act. If he allowed, she was prepared to curb Viswamitra’s pride
and strength, drawing upon the spiritual power instilled in her by Vasistha himself.

__data__.text:
Vasistha acknowledged Viswamitra’s strength as a king and a Kshatriya, pointing out the vast army accompanying him,
filled with elephants, horses, and chariots. Sabala, however, emphasized that the strength of a Brahmana—spiritual and
rooted in wisdom—surpasses the physical might of a Kshatriya. Reassuring Vasistha of his unmatched power, she requested his permission
to defend against Viswamitra’s aggression.
Encouraged by Vasistha, Sabala produced a host of warriors from her powerful bellow. These fierce Pahlava warriors attacked Viswamitra’s army,
swiftly reducing it under his watchful eyes. Enraged, Viswamitra retaliated with his own weapons, scattering the Pahlavas. In response,
Sabala summoned the Sakas, another powerful and numerous group, which covered the land like a flood.
The Sakas, clad in bright garments and wielding sharp swords, fought with immense power,
consuming Viswamitra’s forces as fire consumes dry wood. Countering this, Viswamitra unleashed powerful missiles,
throwing Sabala’s Yavanas, Kambojas, and Barbaras into confusion. The two forces clashed fiercely, each seeking to overpower the other.

Seeing Viswamitra’s newly created warriors scattered and bewildered by Viswamitra’s missile attacks,
Vasistha commanded Sabala to summon even more warriors. In response, Sabala produced a range of powerful and fierce warriors,
each emerging from various parts of her being, including the Kambojas, Barbaras, Yavanas, and Mlecchas, who swiftly eliminated
Viswamitra’s army of foot soldiers, elephants, horses, and chariots.
Witnessing the destruction of his army, Viswamitra’s hundred sons, armed and furious, charged at Vasistha.
However, Vasistha, with a single resounding roar, reduced them all to ashes in an instant, along with their horses and chariots.
Overwhelmed with grief and shame, Viswamitra, feeling stripped of all his power and purpose, withdrew,
entrusting his remaining son with the kingdom’s responsibilities. He then set out alone to the Himalayas to undertake severe penance,
aiming to win Lord Siva’s favor.
After a period of intense austerity, Lord Siva appeared before Viswamitra, acknowledging his devotion and offering a boon.
With humility, Viswamitra requested from the god the complete knowledge of archery, including its deepest secrets and auxiliary sciences,
hoping to enhance his strength and achieve his aspirations.

__data__.text:
After undertaking austerities on the slopes of the Himalayas, Viswamitra finally gained the favor of Lord Siva,
who offered him a boon. Viswamitra humbly requested mastery over divine missiles and the secrets of archery,
along with knowledge known to celestial and supernatural beings alike. Pleased, Lord Siva granted his request,
bestowing upon Viswamitra the power and knowledge he sought before departing.
Empowered with these divine weapons, Viswamitra’s pride grew immensely. Believing himself to be invincible,
he returned to Vasistha's hermitage and unleashed a barrage of missiles, setting the peaceful forest ablaze.
Alarmed, the sages, animals, and students of Vasistha fled in all directions, leaving the grove deserted.
Vasistha called out for calm, assuring the fleeing beings of his protection, and vowed to put an end to Viswamitra's rampage,
likening his intent to the sun dispelling fog.
With an intense and righteous anger, Vasistha lifted his staff, a powerful symbol of his ascetic might,
which shone like a weapon of divine justice. He confronted Viswamitra, condemning him for his attack on the sanctuary,
declaring that his reckless actions marked him as a misguided soul, and that he would soon face the consequences.

__data__.text:
Viswamitra, having obtained formidable mystic weapons, unleashed them upon Vasistha,
challenging him with powerful missiles presided over by various gods. Vasistha, undeterred, raised his Brahmanical staff,
which radiated spiritual power, and stood resolute. Viswamitra, spurred on by his warrior’s pride,
launched a series of powerful celestial weapons, from fiery missiles to those governed by gods like Varuna, Rudra, Indra, and Siva,
each meant to overwhelm Vasistha. Yet, to the amazement of all, Vasistha neutralized each weapon with ease using his staff,
rendering their might ineffective.
Growing increasingly frustrated, Viswamitra released an even greater array of mystic missiles,
including those with powers to stupefy, induce sleep, bring inebriation, generate intense heat, drain moisture, and even rend objects apart.
He used revered weapons like Indra's thunderbolt, Siva's Pinaka, and missiles associated with deities of virtue and time.
Yet, even as Viswamitra’s anger mounted, each missile was calmly subdued by Vasistha's staff, which wielded unmatched spiritual potency.
Desperate and furious, Viswamitra finally summoned Brahmastra, the ultimate weapon presided over by Brahma,
which shook the heavens and alarmed the three worlds. The gods, sages, and celestial beings watched
in trepidation as the Brahmastra’s immense power was unleashed. But Vasistha, unshaken, wielded his staff with his innate Brahmanical glory,
neutralizing the Brahmastra entirely and leaving it powerless.

After Viswamitra's relentless barrage of divine missiles was neutralized, he summoned the Brahmastra,
the ultimate weapon presided over by Brahma. The unleashing of this weapon caused great alarm across the three worlds;
gods, sages, Gandharvas, and celestial beings were awestruck and filled with dread. However, Vasistha, unwavering and calm,
wielded his Brahmanical staff, empowered by his spiritual glory, and neutralized even the Brahmastra entirely.
As Vasistha consumed the Brahmastra, his appearance became fierce and awe-inspiring, casting a powerful aura that mystified the three worlds.
Rays of fire emitted from his skin, while his Brahmanical staff blazed intensely, likened to a rod of ultimate destruction.
The sages, witnessing this extraordinary sight, praised Vasistha’s unmatched spiritual power
and implored him to subdue his formidable energy for the sake of the world.
Moved by their pleas, Vasistha returned to a state of calm, his might fully restrained.
Viswamitra, exhausted and defeated, acknowledged the undeniable superiority of Brahmanical power over martial strength.
Realizing that all his weapons had been rendered ineffective by Vasistha's single staff, Viswamitra admitted the limits of his own might.
Accepting the need for a higher spiritual pursuit, he resolved to undertake rigorous austerities to achieve the transcendence and
wisdom he had witnessed in Vasistha, aspiring ultimately to attain Brahmanhood.

__data__.text:
Distressed and humiliated by his failure to overpower Vasistha, Viswamitra, with a heavy heart,
turned toward the southern region accompanied by his queen, dedicating himself to rigorous austerities.
He survived on fruits and roots, keeping his mind and senses completely controlled, and soon after beginning this intense path,
he fathered four sons, each devoted to truth and virtue: Havispanda, Madhuspanda, Drdhanetra, and Maharatha.
After a thousand years of austerities, Brahma, the creator, appeared and acknowledged Viswamitra’s achievements,
granting him the title of "royal sage" but not Brahmanhood. Disheartened by the recognition falling short of his goal,
Viswamitra resolved to continue his ascetic journey, believing he had yet to achieve true Brahmanical status.
At the same time, King TriSanku of Ayodhya, renowned for his piety and control over his senses, harbored the desire
to perform a sacrifice that would allow him to ascend bodily to heaven. Summoning Vasistha for assistance,
TriSanku shared his intentions, but Vasistha declined, stating it was impossible. Disappointed,
TriSanku sought out Vasistha’s sons in the southern quarter where they were deeply engaged in their own ascetic practices.
With humility and respect, TriSanku approached Vasistha’s sons, hoping they might aid him in fulfilling his aspiration.
Greeting each with due reverence, he humbly requested their support, expressing his vulnerability and seeking their protection.

Having been refused by the noble Vasistha, TriSanku sought out Vasistha's sons in the hope they would assist him with his sacrifice.
Upon finding them in their austere practices, TriSanku humbly greeted each one with respect, concealing his disappointment
and shame from his previous rejection. Bowing before the sons of his revered preceptor, he asked for their support,
acknowledging them as protectors and placing his trust in them for guidance.
He expressed his deep desire to perform a great sacrifice that would allow him to ascend bodily to heaven.
TriSanku entreated them to bless his endeavor and, bowing with sincerity, implored them to grant him permission.
He conveyed his sense of refuge, explaining that after being denied by Vasistha, they were his last hope to achieve this extraordinary goal.
He appealed to their sense of duty toward the Ikswaku dynasty, reminding them of the pivotal role of their father, Vasistha,
as a spiritual guide to his ancestors, and recognized the sons as the next trusted protectors of his lineage.

The sons of Sage Vasistha, enraged by Trisanku’s persistence after their father’s refusal,
chastise him for seeking another patron despite being rejected by a revered and truthful sage.
They reiterate that Sage Vasistha, as the Ikswaku family’s priest, has the final word in such matters,

His followers, horrified by his altered form, abandon him.
Alone and in despair, Trisanku seeks out Viswamitra, whose compassionate nature is stirred by the king’s plight.
Seeing Trisanku reduced to this pitiable state, Viswamitra addresses him kindly and inquires about the purpose of his visit.

stating that despite his adherence to duty and truth, his efforts to ascend to heaven in his bodily form through
a hundred sacrifices have been thwarted. He laments the power of fate, which, in his view, has overshadowed his personal efforts

Following all the prescribed rituals, Viswamitra invokes the gods to accept their offerings.

In his rage, Viswamitra, deeply offended by the gods' refusal to honor his sacrifice, invokes his ascetic powers.
With a fierce declaration of his own spiritual strength, he lifts the sacrificial ladle and assures Trisanku that he will send him
to heaven bodily, overriding the gods’ lack of support. Under Viswamitra’s potent invocation, Trisanku rises to heaven in his physical form,
witnessed by the sages present. However, once Trisanku reaches the celestial realm, Indra and other deities intercept him,
commanding him to return to earth, as he has not earned a rightful place in paradise.
As Trisanku begins to fall headfirst, pleading for Viswamitra’s help, the sage, determined to uphold his promise,
uses his power to suspend Trisanku mid-air, proclaiming that he will create a new realm for him if the gods refuse to accept him.
With a surge of spiritual energy, Viswamitra creates a new constellation and even contemplates forming a parallel realm
governed by an alternative Indra, expressing his resolve to establish Trisanku’s place in heaven.
The gods and sages, alarmed by the magnitude of Viswamitra’s power and the potential consequences,
respectfully implore him to reconsider. They explain that Trisanku’s celestial exile was due to a curse
from his former preceptor and urge Viswamitra to relent. Acknowledging the plea but unwavering in his commitment,
Viswamitra insists that his vow to Trisanku must be honored. He requests that the heavens allow Trisanku a permanent position
among the stars in his physical form.
Ultimately, the gods yield to Viswamitra’s unbreakable resolve, agreeing to let Trisanku remain in a new celestial region,
with stars and constellations surrounding him. This compromise brings harmony, and all the gods, along with the sages,
express gratitude to Viswamitra and return to their realms in peace.

and the chief priest advised the king that a human substitute should be procured to fulfill the ritual requirements.
Taking heed, Ambarisa set off on a search across regions, bringing many cows as offerings for a possible exchange.
In his search, Ambarisa arrived at the sage Rcika’s hermitage and respectfully requested the sage
to sell one of his sons in exchange for a hundred thousand cows. The sage, however, refused to part with his eldest son,
and his wife insisted on the same.

With great reverence, King Ambarisa humbly requested the sage Rcika, asking if he would be willing
to sell one of his sons in exchange for a hundred thousand cows. Ambarisa explained that he had searched all lands
to find the sacrificial animal that had gone missing and was willing to accept a human substitute to fulfill his ritual.
Sage Rcika, however, responded that he could not part with his eldest son, and his wife likewise refused to give up their youngest,
whom she held dearest.
Sunahsepa, their middle son, then spoke up voluntarily, saying,
"Since my father has declared the eldest unsellable and my mother the youngest, I am willing to be given in their place."
King Ambarisa, deeply appreciative of Sunahsepa’s offer, accepted with gratitude. He provided the sage
with numerous riches—gold, silver, precious stones, and countless cattle—and, with Sunahsepa now in his care,
he departed with great satisfaction. Placing Sunahsepa in his chariot, Ambarisa set out quickly to return to his capital.

After taking Sunahsepa with him, King Ambarisa rested at Puskara. While the king was resting, Sunahsepa approached his uncle,
the sage Viswamitra, who was engaged in meditation there. Distressed and fatigued,
Sunahsepa sought refuge in Viswamitra's lap and asked for his protection, saying he had no family left to help him.
He requested Viswamitra to find a way for both him to be saved and for the king’s sacrifice to be completed.
Moved by his nephew's plight, Viswamitra consoled Sunahsepa and then appealed to his own sons,
urging them to assist the boy by volunteering in his place for the sacrificial ritual,
thereby upholding the family's honor and duty to assist others. However, Viswamitra's sons responded dismissively,
questioning why he would consider helping someone else’s son over his own. Their words, laced with reluctance and pride,
greatly angered Viswamitra, who saw their refusal as an affront to piety and duty.

both the sacrifice could proceed successfully, and Sunahsepa would find a protector. However, Viswamitra's sons, led by Madhucchanda,

Turning to Sunahsepa, Viswamitra comforted him and taught him two sacred hymns,
instructing him on how to recite them during the ritual to seek the favor of Indra and Vishnu.

granted him a long life. King Ambarisa, too, was blessed by Indra, achieving the fruits of his sacrifice without harm to Sunahsepa.
Following this, Viswamitra resumed his deep austerities at Puskara, continuing his spiritual practices.

After a thousand years of austerities, all the gods, led by Brahma, approach Viswamitra to grant him the fruits of his devotion,
formally recognizing him as a Rsi, or sage, due to his pious acts and perseverance. Satisfied, Brahma returns to the heavens,

After some time, Menaka, a beautiful celestial nymph, arrives at Puskara to bathe. Viswamitra, taken by her beauty,
invites her to stay in his hermitage, succumbing to desire. For ten years, they live together in contentment, but eventually,
Viswamitra realizes he has been distracted from his spiritual path, sensing that this was part of the gods' plan to disrupt his focus.
With remorse and frustration, he understands that he has been led astray by passion.
Determined to regain control, Viswamitra dismisses Menaka gently and heads to the Himalayas
to dedicate himself anew to a life of strict celibacy and spiritual discipline. He commits
to intense austerities along the banks of the Kausiki River, drawing the attention and concern of the gods,
who see his renewed devotion as formidable. All the gods, accompanied by the Rsis, approach Brahma,

determined to resume his path of spiritual discipline. He reaches the Kausiki River and resolves to conquer his desires,
dedicating himself to severe austerities that astonish even the gods. Disturbed by the intensity of Viswamitra's devotion,
the gods appeal to Brahma to bestow a suitable title on him.
Responding to their plea, Brahma commends Viswamitra, addressing him as a distinguished Rsi.
Yet Viswamitra humbly requests the esteemed title of Brahmarsi, signifying ultimate spiritual mastery.
Brahma, noting Viswamitra’s sincerity but cautioning that he has yet to conquer all desires, encourages him to persist.
Following this, Brahma returns to the heavens, and Viswamitra resumes his rigorous austerities.
With unmatched resolve, Viswamitra endures extreme conditions: standing amidst four fires in the summer,
remaining unsheltered during rains, and meditating in icy waters through the winter. His asceticism,
unshaken for a thousand years, creates growing anxiety among the gods, who, led by Indra, decide to intervene once more.
They summon the celestial nymph Rambha to distract Viswamitra, hoping to curb his rising spiritual power.

by awakening his passions. Rambha, hesitant and fearful of the sage's temper, pleads with Indra,
expressing her reluctance and fear of incurring a curse from Viswamitra. However, Indra reassures her, promising that he will be close by,
disguised as a cuckoo, and that together they can create an atmosphere of beauty and charm to distract the sage.
Reluctantly, Rambha agrees. She assumes an enchanting appearance and approaches Viswamitra, who soon hears the sweet,
alluring song of the cuckoo, which, combined with Rambha’s presence, starts to draw his attention. For a moment,
he becomes uncertain about her intentions, suspecting that this might be another attempt by Indra to disturb his penance.
Realizing the nature of this plan, Viswamitra’s anger flares up, and he pronounces a severe curse on Rambha,
condemning her to turn into stone for ten thousand years as punishment for attempting to disrupt his spiritual journey.
He adds that she will only be released from this state by a Brahmana of great virtue and power. Following this curse,
Viswamitra feels a deep sense of remorse, recognizing that his reaction has weakened the spiritual merit he had accumulated.
Immediately, Rambha is transformed into stone, and Indra and the god of love quickly retreat, dismayed by the outcome.

The gods express concern, noting that Viswamitra’s unyielding discipline and flawless conduct have made him a force

to prevent potential destruction. With a deep respect for his commitment and mindful of his powerful ascetic energy,
Brahma and the gods finally approach Viswamitra, addressing him with honor and granting him the title of Brahmana Rsi
in acknowledgment of his extraordinary spiritual accomplishments.

but Janaka declared that she could only be won by one who could prove his strength with Shiva's bow.
The bow was then brought forth for all the princes to attempt,
establishing the challenge of valor that awaited any suitor seeking Sita’s hand in marriage.

Janaka recounts how, pleased with the gods' reconciliation, they entrusted the bow to his ancestor, Devarata.
Continuing, he describes how, while plowing a sacred field, he found a baby girl, whom he named Sita, emerging from the earth.
Janaka raised Sita with great affection, pledging that she would marry a suitor of extraordinary valor.
Many kings came forward, seeking her hand, but Janaka maintained that only one who could lift
and string the divine bow of Shiva would be deemed worthy.
In their attempts to lift the bow, none of the princes could even shift it, revealing their strength to be insufficient.
Frustrated by their failure, the kings grew angry, besieging Mithila in retaliation,
which led to a prolonged conflict that depleted the city’s resources. Desperate, Janaka sought divine intervention,
and the gods responded by granting him a powerful army. With this support, he was able to repel the hostile kings,

Janaka pledges to give Sita, his cherished daughter born of the earth, in marriage to him, fulfilling his promise of valor.

DaSaratha explained that the sage Vasistha, an esteemed spiritual guide of the Ikswaku dynasty,
would recount his family’s history. Vasistha then began narrating the lineage, tracing it back to Brahma,
the eternal creator. Brahma’s lineage included Marici, Kasyapa, Vivaswan (the sun-god), and Manu,
the lord of all beings, from whom the Ikswaku dynasty originated. Ikswaku was noted as the first ruler of Ayodhya.
Continuing the lineage, Vasistha named Kuksi, Vikuksi, and Bana, all great kings
who were renowned for their virtues and strength. The line continued with Anaranya, Prthu, Trisanku, and Dhundhumara,
each a famed leader of his time. Dhundhumara’s son, Yuvanaswa, fathered Mandhata, a celebrated king,
who had sons including Susandhi, followed by Dhruvasandhi and Prasenjit. The lineage carried forward through Bharata,
and then Asita, who faced rivalries from other noble families, yet the Ikswaku dynasty continued
its legacy of courage and righteousness.

Vasistha continued narrating the lineage of the Ikswaku dynasty, describing the descendants of King Dhundhumara.
Yuvanaswa, a great warrior, fathered Mandhata, whose son, Susandhi, had two sons named Dhruvasandhi and Prasenjit.
Dhruvasandhi’s son was Bharata, who fathered Asita, a powerful ruler who encountered fierce opposition from rival clans.
After losing his kingdom in battle, Asita retreated to the Himalayas with his two wives and passed away.
One of Asita’s wives, pregnant and wishing for a son, sought blessings from the sage Cyavana, who resided nearby.
Her co-wife, however, gave her food laced with poison in an attempt to harm the unborn child. Cyavana reassured her,
foretelling that she would give birth to a son of exceptional strength and glory despite the poison.
Thus, the child was named Sagara, symbolizing his resilience. Sagara’s lineage included sons like
Asamanja, Amsuman, and eventually Bhagiratha, renowned for his dedication and achievements.
The line continued with notable kings such as Kakutstha, Raghu,
Pravrddha (who became known as Kalmasapada due to a curse), and other illustrious descendants like
Sudarsana, Agnivarna, and Ambarisa. From Ambarisa descended Nahusha, who fathered Yayati, then Nabhaga, and finally Aja,
the father of King Dasaratha.
Vasistha concluded by reminding King Janaka of the purity, honor, and valor upheld by the Ikswaku dynasty.
Representing Dasaratha, Vasistha requested that Janaka offer his two daughters in marriage to Dasaratha's sons,
Rama and Lakshmana, as they were worthy companions for Janaka’s esteemed daughters.

Janaka, with respect and reverence, responded to Vasistha’s words, agreeing to recount his own lineage as per tradition.
He explained that in matters of marriage, especially when offering one’s daughter to a suitor,
it is essential to recite the family history in detail.
Janaka began with Nimi, a virtuous and renowned king, respected in all three realms. His son was Mithi,
from whom the title “Janaka” originated. Mithi’s descendants included notable kings:
Udavasu, Nandivardhana, and Suketu, each known for their strength and piety. Suketu’s son was Devarata,
famed for his might, followed by Brhadratha, Mahavira, and Sudhrti, all valiant leaders in their own right.
Continuing, Janaka listed subsequent generations, including Dhrstaketu, Haryaswa, Maru, Pratindhaka, Kirtiratha,
and Devamidha, all recognized for their righteousness and strength. The lineage led to Vibudha, Mahidhraka, Kirtirata,
and Maharoma, eventually reaching Janaka’s father, Hraswaroma.
Hraswaroma had two sons, Janaka himself and his younger brother, Kusadhwaja.
After appointing Janaka as the king and entrusting him with Kusadhwaja’s care, their father retired to the forest,
living a life of renunciation. Following his father’s passing, Janaka fulfilled his duties as ruler with righteousness,
protecting Kusadhwaja like a divine figure.
Later, King Sudhanva of Sankasya arrived, laying siege to Mithila, which marked a pivotal event in Janaka’s reign.

King Janaka continued by affirming that the four royal princes should marry the four princesses on the same day.
He suggested that the most auspicious timing for the wedding would be under the Phalguni constellations,
an alignment favored by the wise and presided over by Prajapati. Rising respectfully,
Janaka thanked the sages for honoring his family with this alliance, expressing that the gift of his daughters
to such noble suitors filled him with gratitude. He invited the sages to be seated in honor and assured them that
Mithila and Ayodhya were now united in kinship.
As Janaka spoke, King Dasaratha, pleased, expressed admiration for Janaka and his brother Kusadhwaja,
commending their generosity and virtues. He then requested permission to retire to his residence to perform the Sraddha,
a ritual of respect for his ancestors.
Upon returning to his lodging, Dasaratha completed the Sraddha rites with full ceremony and,
the next morning, observed the Samavartana ritual, marking a coming-of-age rite for his sons.
In celebration, he generously distributed gifts, offering a hundred thousand cows to Brahmanas for each son and
presenting four hundred thousand cows with golden horns and ample milk, along with many other treasures.
Surrounded by his sons, Dasaratha appeared radiant, akin to Brahma amidst the divine guardians of the cosmos,
as he honored the sages and marked this momentous union of their families.

He respectfully greeted King Dasaratha, conveying the well wishes of his father and expressing his eagerness to see Bharata.

Welcoming Yudhajit as an honored guest, Dasaratha provided him with the highest hospitality.

He was joined by his sons, all dressed in splendid, ceremonial attire adorned with fine ornaments,
as they arrived at the auspicious hour known as Vijaya.
With Vasistha at the head, the sage addressed Janaka, acknowledging that the preparations were complete and requesting that

Janaka affirmed that his daughters were ready at the sacrificial altar, adorned for the occasion and awaiting the ceremony.
Assuring that Mithila was as much Dasaratha's domain as his own, he encouraged the proceedings without delay,
expressing that all was prepared for the blessed union.

Upon Vasistha’s respectful request, King Janaka, with a profound sense of righteousness and nobility,
declared his openness to the sacred wedding proceedings. He emphasized that there should be no hesitation,
welcoming all as though they were in their own home. Confidently, he affirmed that his daughters, adorned and ready,
were already seated near the sacrificial altar.
Following Janaka's words, Dasaratha led his sons and the assembled sages into the ceremonial pavilion.
Janaka then addressed Vasistha, respectfully requesting him to conduct the wedding ceremony of Rama and his brothers
according to tradition. In response, Vasistha, joined by Viswamitra and other revered sages
prepared the sacred altar at the center of the pavilion. He adorned it with fragrant sandalwood paste,
flowers, golden plates, and jars filled with auspicious items. After meticulously arranging various ceremonial vessels,
he covered the altar with blades of Darbha grass and lit the ritual fire, offering oblations with recited hymns.
With the preparations complete, Janaka brought forward Sita, beautifully adorned in wedding attire.
Seating her across from Rama, he addressed him with words of reverence, announcing Sita as his beloved daughter
and expressing that she was prepared to stand by him in fulfilling his sacred duties.

With Sita, adorned in fine jewels, comfortably seated before the sacred fire opposite Sri Rama,
King Janaka addressed Rama with deep reverence, presenting Sita as his beloved daughter and
Rama's destined partner in fulfilling sacred duties. Janaka urged Rama to accept Sita’s hand,
blessing their union and assuring that she would remain a devoted and steadfast companion.
Janaka then symbolically poured consecrated water into Rama’s hands, signifying the formal offering of Sita to him.
In response, a joyous echo arose from the gods and sages, accompanied by celestial music and a shower of divine flowers.
After this, Janaka invited Lakshmana to take Urmila’s hand, and similarly urged Bharata and Shatrughna
to accept the hands of Mandavi and Srutakirti. Blessing them all, Janaka emphasized that the auspicious hour should not be delayed.
Following Vasistha’s guidance, each prince took his bride’s hand, and together they circled the sacrificial fire
and altar in the traditional clockwise direction, formally completing the wedding rites as prescribed by the scriptures.
The celebration was magnificent, with celestial music resounding and heavenly flowers raining down,
as divine nymphs danced and the heavenly musicians sang.
The joyful scene was filled with blessings and harmonious sounds, as each prince, along with his bride,
performed the final ritual circling of the fire three times. Then, accompanied by their new brides,
the princes retired to their tents, followed by King Dasaratha, the sages, and all the gathered relatives,
all sharing in the happiness of this sacred union.

As dawn approached, the revered sage Viswamitra took leave of both King Janaka and King Dasaratha and
set off toward the northern mountains, returning to his hermitage. Shortly after Viswamitra’s departure,
King Dasaratha, seeking Janaka’s permission, also prepared to return to Ayodhya with his sons and their newly-wedded brides.
In a grand gesture, Janaka provided an abundant dowry, including countless fine garments, adorned servants,
livestock, gold, pearls, and other riches, all gifted joyfully to his daughters and their husbands.
With these gifts presented, Janaka returned to Mithila, while Dasaratha, accompanied by sages and his entourage,
began his journey back to Ayodhya.
As they traveled, ominous signs appeared. Fearsome birds circled, calling out harshly,
while deer crossed the path from the left, creating a mix of foreboding and blessing. Troubled by these signs,
Dasaratha consulted Vasistha, who interpreted the sounds as warnings of impending danger. Amid their conversation,
a sudden storm struck, shaking the earth, uprooting trees, and casting an intense darkness that obscured all directions.
In this chaotic atmosphere, the members of Dasaratha’s entourage were nearly overcome. Only the sages, the king,
and his sons remained aware amidst the confusion. Emerging from the darkness, they beheld the formidable figure of Parasurama,
the mighty sage and warrior, bearing an axe and bow. His presence was as intense as a blazing fire,
his form intimidating and powerful, akin to Lord Shiva in strength and appearance.

As Dasaratha and his party journeyed onward, Vasistha observed that the appearance of deer was a positive sign,
encouraging Dasaratha to let go of his anxiety. However, their peace was interrupted by a sudden,
intense storm that swept through, shaking the ground and toppling trees. Darkness enveloped the sun, leaving all unsure of their path.
In the thick dust, most of the party fell into confusion, with only Vasistha, Dasaratha, and his sons retaining awareness.
In the midst of this chaos, they saw Parasurama, a fearsome and radiant figure,
standing before them. With matted locks and wielding an axe and bow, his presence was both commanding and intimidating,
as formidable as a mountain or a raging fire. His fierce appearance, glowing with power, reminded the party of Lord Shiva.
Gathering courage, the sages, including Vasistha, observed the sage Parasurama. They wondered if he,
once known for his vow to rid the world of the Ksatriya race, would seek vengeance once more. Speaking amongst themselves,
they noted that Parasurama's past anger had been appeased after avenging his father's death.
They hoped he would not bring further destruction.
With cautious respect, the sages approached Parasurama, offering him ritual water and addressing him with the greeting,
"Rama, O Rama," in a gentle tone. Accepting this welcome, Parasurama then addressed Sri Rama, Dasaratha’s eldest son,
with great gravity, signaling the beginning of a significant encounter.

Parasurama promises him a duel to honor his valor.

he implores Parasurama to restrain his anger toward the Ksatriyas. He reminds Parasurama of his own peaceful vows as a sage
and his commitment to non-violence after renouncing the earth’s dominion to Sage Kasyapa.
Despite Dasaratha’s plea, Parasurama, resolute and unwavering, addresses only Rama.
He explains that two celestial bows of immense power were created by the divine craftsman Viswakarma.
One of these was bestowed upon Lord Shiva, which Rama recently shattered. The other, belonging to Lord Vishnu,
is now in Parasurama’s possession. He presents this bow, which has the power to vanquish enemies,
inviting Rama to prove his strength with it.

Parasurama elaborates on the history of two extraordinary bows crafted by the divine Viswakarma, revered across the cosmos.
One of these, now broken by Rama, was originally given to Lord Shiva to defeat the demon Tripura, symbolizing its immense power.
The second bow, in Parasurama's possession, was entrusted to Lord Vishnu.
Both these bows represent celestial strength and are revered by gods and sages alike.
Recalling an ancient rivalry, Parasurama tells of a fierce contest between Shiva and Vishnu,
a battle so intense that the bow of Shiva was rendered inactive by Vishnu’s overpowering roar.
Witnessing this, the gods intervened, persuading Shiva and Vishnu to reconcile. Recognizing Vishnu’s might,
the gods entrusted these sacred weapons to two great sages. Shiva’s bow went to the royal sage Devarata,
while Vishnu’s was given to Rcika, Parasurama's ancestor.
Continuing the tale, Parasurama recounts how his father, the sage Jamadagni, inherited Vishnu’s bow but was killed by Sahasrabahu,
a Kshatriya king, despite his peaceful nature. In response, Parasurama vowed vengeance, systematically challenging the Kshatriyas.
After a period of conquest, he eventually renounced his victories, offering the earth to Sage Kasyapa as a sacrificial gift.
Having retreated to Mount Mahendra, Parasurama returned upon hearing of Rama's feat in breaking Shiva's bow.
Now, he challenges Rama to prove his valor with Vishnu's bow. Instructing Rama to fit an arrow to it,
Parasurama promises to engage him in single combat, testing the strength of this descendant of the Ikshvaku lineage.
